title: Heavy Marijuana Smoking and Cancer Risk
hook: Growing research links heavy marijuana smoking to a higher risk of lung and head-and-neck cancers — though scientists still don't know how much use is enough to meaningfully raise that risk.
key_points: Growing research links heavy marijuana smoking to a higher risk of lung cancer and several head and neck cancers.
Scientists haven't yet determined how much use is enough to significantly raise cancer risk.
Edibles have not been linked to lung cancer so far, unlike smoked marijuana.
The long-term effects of vaping marijuana and secondhand marijuana smoke are still being investigated.
content_html: Marijuana's cancer-risk profile is still being filled in, but a growing body of research points in one clear direction: heavy smoking of it appears to raise the risk of lung cancer and several head and neck cancers, according to ScienceDaily.
extra_html: What's still unresolved matters just as much as what's known. Researchers haven't pinned down how much marijuana use is enough to meaningfully raise cancer risk, and the picture changes by method: edibles haven't been linked to lung cancer so far, since they skip the inhaled combustion byproducts that come with smoking, while the long-term effects of vaping marijuana and exposure to secondhand marijuana smoke are still being actively investigated. For now, the clearest signal is the oldest one in tobacco research too — smoking something, heavily and over time, tends to carry more risk than other ways of using it.

related.title: Vaping and Cancer: The Evidence Is Mounting
related.hook: A major review concludes nicotine vapes are likely to cause lung and oral cancers — challenging the idea that vaping is a harmless alternative to smoking.

related.title: Teen Cannabis Use and Serious Mental Illness
related.hook: A study of more than 463,000 adolescents tied teen cannabis use to roughly double the risk of serious mental illness — and the use usually came first.

related.title: Quitting Smoking
related.hook: Your body starts repairing itself within hours of your last cigarette. Quitting is hard and relapse is common — but the right support roughly doubles your odds of success.

flashcards.back_html: A higher risk of lung cancer and several head and neck cancers — though how much use is needed to meaningfully raise that risk is still unclear.

flashcards.prompt: How does the cancer-risk picture differ between smoked marijuana and edibles, per current research?

choices.text: Edibles haven't been linked to lung cancer so far, unlike smoked marijuana
Edibles carry the same lung cancer risk as smoking
Neither form has ever been studied for cancer risk

flashcards.explanation_html: Lung cancer risk research so far centers on smoked marijuana; edibles haven't shown the same link, since they don't involve inhaling combustion byproducts.
